You are walking down the street and you suddenly see something so shocking — a building on fire, a celebrity, an enormous snake — that your jaw drops open and you freeze, staring. You are not doing this on purpose. Your body just reacts. That frozen, open-mouthed stare is the heart of the word gape.
Meaning 1: To Stare Open-Mouthed in Shock, Surprise, or Wonder

This is the most common meaning of the word. When you gape at something or someone, you stare at them with your mouth hanging open, usually because you are so surprised, shocked, amazed, or fascinated that you cannot help it.

Three things make gaping different from ordinary staring:

  1. Your mouth is open. It is not just your eyes that are wide — your whole face has gone slack with surprise.
  2. You cannot look away. Gaping is a sustained, fixed stare — not a quick glance. You are locked in.
  3. You have lost control of your reaction. This is key. Gaping is involuntary. Nobody decides to gape. It just happens to you when something overwhelms your senses.

Examples:

  • She gaped at the size of the mansion.
  • The crowd gaped as the stuntman leaped from the building.
  • He gaped at her, unable to find words.
  • The children gaped in wonder at the fireworks.

Notice that you always gape at something, or gape in a feeling (wonder, horror, disbelief). These are the natural pairings.

Social tone: Gaping is often considered slightly rude or unsophisticated. If you say someone was "gaping" at a person, you subtly suggest they lacked the self-control to look away politely. It is not a dignified thing to do — it is an exposed, unguarded reaction. This is why writers use the word to show a character is caught completely off guard or is behaving without restraint.
Meaning 2: To Be Wide Open (Said of Objects, Spaces, or Openings)

The second meaning applies not to people, but to things. When an opening, hole, wound, or gap gapes, it is wide open — spread apart in a way that is large, exposed, and often alarming or striking. Think of it as the object "yawning" open.

Examples:

  • A large wound gaped on his leg. (The wound was wide open, not closed.)
  • A hole gaped in the ceiling where the roof had caved in.
  • The canyon gaped before them, hundreds of metres deep.
  • Her coat had a tear that gaped open every time she moved.

This meaning is closely connected to the adjective gaping, which you will encounter very frequently — as in "a gaping wound," "a gaping hole," or "a gaping chasm." These all describe something wide open, exposed, and impossible to ignore.

Both meanings share one single core idea: something that is wide open and impossible to ignore.

In Meaning 1, it is the person's mouth that is wide open — out of shock or awe.
In Meaning 2, it is the thing itself (a hole, a wound, a gap) that is wide open.

Once you hold that image — wide open, exposed, demanding your attention — you will always understand what "gape" means, no matter how it is used.

UseWhat it means
A person gapesThey stare open-mouthed, frozen by shock, surprise, or wonder
A thing gapesIt is wide open, yawning, spread apart in a large and striking way
One Tip to Remember It Forever

Think of the word gap sitting inside gape. Both words are about an opening. "Gap" is the noun (the opening itself), and "gape" is the verb (the act of being or making that opening — whether it is a mouth hanging open or a hole torn wide).
